intro: Oahu's most remarkable trees cluster in eleven places. Foster Botanical Garden holds five behind one modest entrance fee: a baobab, a Bodhi tree of the Bodh Gaya lineage, a kapok older than the garden, a cannonball tree and a quipo. Moanalua Gardens keeps the Hitachi Tree, famous from Japanese television, under its own ticket. Everything else is free: banyans at Thomas Square, the Honolulu Zoo gate, the Moana hotel's courtyard and the International Market Place, a monkeypod in Nuuanu Valley Park, three trees on the UH Manoa campus, and a baobab and a pink bombax at Queen's Medical Center.
meta_description: Oahu's most remarkable trees: a baobab and a Bodhi tree in one Honolulu garden, the Hitachi Tree at Moanalua, a palace banyan and free hospital giants.
question_meta: Oahu's oldest confirmed tree is a kapok planted around 1851 in Foster Botanical Garden, roughly 175 years old. Full list of 19.
question_answer: Oahu's oldest documented tree is the Hillebrand Kapok in Foster Botanical Garden, planted around 1851 by the garden's founder, William Hillebrand, on what was then his own homestead. That makes it roughly 175 years old, older than the garden itself.
question_context: Foster Botanical Garden holds five of the nineteen trees on this page, and its own founding is younger than its oldest tree. William Hillebrand planted a kapok on his Honolulu homestead around 1851, decades before it became a public garden; it now stands about 27 metres tall with a trunk somewhere between four and seven metres around, the two sources disagreeing. Two more carry documented dates: a Bodhi tree of the Bodh Gaya lineage, given to Mary Foster in 1913, and a baobab planted in the 1930s, thirteen metres round. Fourteen more trees stand elsewhere, nearly all free: banyans at Thomas Square, the Honolulu Zoo gate, Iolani Palace, the Moana hotel's beachfront courtyard and the Kuhio Beach hula mound; the banyan the International Market Place rebuilt its steel canopy around rather than fell; the Geometry Tree of Ala Moana Beach Park; a monkeypod in Nuuanu Valley Park; a baobab, a cannonball tree and a tree that smells of dung once a year at UH Manoa; and a baobab and a pink bombax at Queen's Medical Center. The Hitachi Tree, famous across Japan as a company emblem, is the one paid exception, at Moanalua Gardens.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Oahu?
faq.a: The Hillebrand Kapok in Foster Botanical Garden, planted around 1851 by the garden's founder before the garden itself existed. It is roughly 175 years old.

faq.q: Where are Oahu's most remarkable trees?
faq.a: Five stand inside Foster Botanical Garden in downtown Honolulu, on the edge of Chinatown, within a five minute walk of each other. The rest stand apart and cost nothing but the Hitachi Tree does: Moanalua Gardens keeps that one under its own ticket, while Thomas Square, Ala Moana Beach Park, the UH Manoa campus, Nuuanu Valley Park, Iolani Palace, Queen's Medical Center, the gate of the Honolulu Zoo, the Moana Surfrider's courtyard and the International Market Place all keep their trees free.

faq.q: Is Foster Botanical Garden free to visit?
faq.a: No. Entry costs $1 to $5 for general admission, $3 for Hawaii residents, with a $25 annual family pass. It is open 9am to 4pm daily except Christmas and New Year's Day.

faq.q: Why do so many of Oahu's remarkable trees grow in one garden?
faq.a: Foster Botanical Garden began as the private collection of William Hillebrand and later Thomas and Mary Foster, who spent decades bringing in botanical curiosities from around the world before the city took the grounds over as a public garden. About twenty five of Oahu's roughly one hundred city-designated Exceptional Trees grow within its fourteen acres.

trees.name: The Foster Garden Baobab

location.address: 180 N. Vineyard Blvd, Honolulu, HI 96817 (Foster Botanical Garden)

verified_sources: https://data.honolulu.gov/resource/84fd-3fzf.json (City and County of Honolulu, Exceptional Trees register, register_id 1)
trees.access: Paid entry: $1-5 general admission, $3 for Hawaii residents, $25 annual family pass. Open 9am-4pm daily except Christmas and New Year's Day.
trees.transport: On N. Vineyard Blvd in downtown Honolulu, on the edge of Chinatown; several TheBus routes run along Vineyard Blvd past the garden entrance.
trees.story:
Honolulu calls this one the Dead Rat Tree. The nickname is the seed pods: grey, furred, hanging on long stalks all around the crown, and once you have seen them you cannot unsee them. Under the pods is an African baobab, planted in Foster Botanical Garden in the 1930s and already carrying a trunk close to thirteen metres around. Ninety-odd years for that waistline is quick work, even for a species that grows a trunk largely to store water in it. The city's Exceptional Trees register gives its height as about twenty metres and rates its condition good.

Baobabs belong to dry African savanna, where they stand bare for months and flower at night for bats. This one has spent its whole life on fourteen acres of downtown Honolulu at the edge of Chinatown, on ground that was a private botanical collection long before the city took it over. It sat out a 1.26 million dollar renovation that closed the garden completely, and was still standing when the gates reopened in August 2023.

About twenty five of Oahu's hundred or so protected Exceptional Trees grow inside these same fourteen acres. That is the argument for the entrance fee: nowhere else on the island puts this many designated trees within a five minute walk of each other.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the grey furred seed pods hanging on long stalks all around the crown, and by a trunk close to thirteen metres round. It stands in Foster Botanical Garden, about twenty metres tall.

trees.name: The Foster Garden Bodhi Tree

location.address: 180 N. Vineyard Blvd, Honolulu, HI 96817 (Foster Botanical Garden)

verified_sources: https://data.honolulu.gov/resource/84fd-3fzf.json (City and County of Honolulu, Exceptional Trees register, register_id 420)
trees.access: Paid entry: $1-5 general admission, $3 for Hawaii residents, $25 annual family pass. Open 9am-4pm daily except Christmas and New Year's Day.
trees.transport: On N. Vineyard Blvd in downtown Honolulu, on the edge of Chinatown; several TheBus routes run along Vineyard Blvd past the garden entrance.
trees.story:
The tree the Buddha is said to have sat under has descendants, and one of them grows in downtown Honolulu. This sacred fig was raised from a cutting of the Bodh Gaya lineage in India and arrived as a sapling in 1913, a gift to Mary Foster from Anagarika Dharmapala, the Sri Lankan reformer who spent his life campaigning to return that Indian temple to Buddhist hands. Foster planted it in her garden and went on to become a major patron of Buddhism in Hawaii, paying for the islands' first Buddhist temple.

The tree is about 113 years old now, roughly fifteen metres tall, with a trunk over seven metres around, and the city's Exceptional Trees register rates its condition excellent. Sacred figs are easy to identify once someone shows you the leaf: heart-shaped, drawn out into a long thin tail, hung so loosely on its stalk that the whole crown moves in air you cannot feel on your own skin. A tree that moves on a still day is the sort of thing people build religions around.

It is one of the few trees in this garden whose value has nothing to do with its size. There are bigger and far stranger specimens within a hundred metres of it. This is the one with a paper trail back to India and a woman who knew exactly what she had been given.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the leaves, heart shaped and drawn out into a long thin tail, hung so loosely that the crown moves on a still day. It stands in Foster Botanical Garden, fifteen metres tall.

trees.name: The Hillebrand Kapok

location.address: 180 N. Vineyard Blvd, Honolulu, HI 96817 (Foster Botanical Garden)

verified_sources: https://data.honolulu.gov/resource/84fd-3fzf.json (City and County of Honolulu, Exceptional Trees register, register_id 116)
trees.access: Paid entry: $1-5 general admission, $3 for Hawaii residents, $25 annual family pass. Open 9am-4pm daily except Christmas and New Year's Day.
trees.transport: On N. Vineyard Blvd in downtown Honolulu, on the edge of Chinatown; several TheBus routes run along Vineyard Blvd past the garden entrance.
trees.story:
The oldest tree in Foster Botanical Garden is older than the garden, because the man who planted it lived here first. William Hillebrand, the German physician and botanist who made this ground his homestead, put a kapok in at around 1851. That gives it roughly 175 years. It was already a mature tree when the Hawaiian Kingdom was overthrown in 1893, and a very large one when Pearl Harbor was bombed.

Its height is not in doubt. Honolulu Magazine and the city's Exceptional Trees register both give 88 and a half feet, about 27 metres, which is also how we know the two are describing the same trunk. The trunk itself they disagree on, and not by a little. The magazine reports 151 inches around, a shade under four metres. The register records 6.98 metres. The two have never been reconciled, so both stand here rather than one being quietly chosen. Some of the gap is probably method: a kapok throws out buttress roots like thin walls, and the answer changes depending on the height at which you measure.

Standing at the base, the buttresses are the point anyway. They rise past head height and divide the ground around the trunk into separate rooms, which is what a rainforest giant does when it has to hold itself up in shallow soil.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the buttress roots, thin walls rising past head height and dividing the ground around the trunk into rooms. It stands in Foster Botanical Garden, 27 metres tall and its oldest tree.

trees.name: The Foster Garden Cannonball Tree

location.address: 180 N. Vineyard Blvd, Honolulu, HI 96817 (Foster Botanical Garden)

verified_sources: https://data.honolulu.gov/resource/84fd-3fzf.json (City and County of Honolulu, Exceptional Trees register, register_id 118)
trees.access: Paid entry: $1-5 general admission, $3 for Hawaii residents, $25 annual family pass. Open 9am-4pm daily except Christmas and New Year's Day.
trees.transport: On N. Vineyard Blvd in downtown Honolulu, on the edge of Chinatown; several TheBus routes run along Vineyard Blvd past the garden entrance.
trees.story:
The garden has put up a sign beside this tree warning visitors about falling cannonballs, and it is not a joke. Couroupita guianensis grows its fruit straight out of the trunk rather than from the branches, woody spheres somewhere between a grapefruit and a shot put, hanging on thick stalks that push out of the bark itself. Botanists call the habit cauliflory. Gravity calls it a hazard. A ripe one comes down from height and splits open with a smell that carries.

The flowers work the same way and are the reason to come: waxy, orange and pink, each one a shell-shaped hood over a dense spray of stamens, opening in ropes down the trunk at eye level while the crown sails on 29 metres above. It is a South American tree, from the Amazon and the Guianas, soft-wooded and fast, and the city's Exceptional Trees register rates this specimen's condition excellent. It is the most straightforwardly strange thing in a garden that is not short of competition.

One thing about it is missing: nobody has recorded when it went into the ground. If you know the planting date, or know someone at the garden who does, tell us and it goes on the page.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the flowers and the woody fruit growing straight out of the trunk at eye level, and by the sign warning about falling cannonballs. It stands in Foster Botanical Garden, 29 metres tall.

trees.name: The Foster Garden Quipo

location.address: 180 N. Vineyard Blvd, Honolulu, HI 96817 (Foster Botanical Garden)

verified_sources: https://data.honolulu.gov/resource/84fd-3fzf.json (City and County of Honolulu, Exceptional Trees register, register_id 114)
trees.access: Paid entry: $1-5 general admission, $3 for Hawaii residents, $25 annual family pass. Open 9am-4pm daily except Christmas and New Year's Day.
trees.transport: On N. Vineyard Blvd in downtown Honolulu, on the edge of Chinatown; several TheBus routes run along Vineyard Blvd past the garden entrance.
trees.story:
This trunk is soft enough to cut with a knife. The quipo comes from the forests of Panama and Colombia, where it grows wood about as dense as balsa and gets felled for rafts and dugout canoes rather than for anything expected to hold weight. The tree wears that wood in a shape to match: smooth, greenish-grey, swollen low down and tapering upward, closer to a water tank than to anything with bark on it. Honolulu Botanical Gardens' own record puts the planting at 1930, which makes this one about 96 years old.

It has reached roughly 26 metres. That figure comes from the city's Exceptional Trees register alone and has not been checked against a second measurement, so treat it as the best number available rather than a settled one. Its seedpods are the other reason to look up: large, papery and winged, built to spin on the way down. The register rates the tree's condition excellent.

It stands near the centre of the garden, which is about right, because it is the specimen most visitors cannot name and cannot walk past either. Nothing else on these fourteen acres looks less like a tree, and that includes a baobab.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, smooth and greenish grey, swollen low down and tapering upward more like a water tank than a tree. It stands near the centre of Foster Botanical Garden.

trees.name: The Hitachi Tree

location.address: Moanalua Gardens, 2850A Moanalua Road, Honolulu, HI 96819

trees.access: Paid entry, Moanalua Gardens admission (10 dollars), daily 08:30 to 16:00
trees.transport: About 8 km from Waikiki; TheBus routes along Moanalua Road stop by the gardens, and there is parking at the gate
trees.story:
This rain tree is on Japanese television most weeks, and almost nobody watching knows it is in Honolulu. Hitachi has used it as the company emblem since 1973, with a jingle that begins "this tree, what tree", and it is famous enough in Japan that visitors arrive at Moanalua Gardens asking for it by the company's name rather than the tree's.

What brought the advertising people here is obvious from the lawn. A rain tree grows outward rather than upward, and this one has spent about 130 years doing it: roughly 25 metres tall and a crown wide enough to shade some three thousand square feet of grass, held up on limbs that reach almost horizontally before turning. Stand under the middle and the canopy closes overhead like a roof.

The leaves do something worth timing your visit for. The leaflets fold shut in the late afternoon and before rain, which is where the name comes from, and the light through the canopy changes completely when they do. Hawaii knows the species as the monkeypod, and that is the name on the sign.

The gardens are privately owned and charge admission, which is unusual for a tree on this site and worth knowing before you drive out. The lawn around the trunk is open, so you can walk right up to it.

trees.name: The Banyans of Thomas Square

location.address: Thomas Square, 925 S Beretania St, Honolulu, HI 96814

trees.access: Free, public city park (Honolulu's oldest, dedicated 1850), open daylight into early evening, no admission.
trees.transport: Downtown Honolulu, at Beretania and Victoria Streets, across from the Honolulu Museum of Art; walkable from Waikiki or reachable by TheBus.
trees.story:
Honolulu's oldest public park did not always have shade. Thomas Square was set aside as parkland in 1850, but the banyans came decades later, when the Scottish merchant Archibald Scott Cleghorn took over as steward in 1882 and brought cuttings from Ainahau, his own Waikiki estate, to plant here. The overhauled park reopened to a brass-band crowd on 7 April 1887, and by the 1930s four banyans ringed the new central fountain, where they still stand.

They are Indian banyans, Ficus benghalensis, named in a University of Hawaii extension guide that singles out this exact grove as the reference specimen for the species in the islands, adding dryly that Disneyland's own banyan nearby is artificial. Cleghorn is better known today as the father of Princess Kaiulani and, later, Governor of Oahu; Ainahau, the estate these cuttings came from, held its own famous banyan, the one under which Robert Louis Stevenson used to read poetry to his young daughter.

Thomas Square has been public land since 1850, protected as a city park since 1925, and free to walk every day, no ticket and no gate, with King Street traffic on one side and the Honolulu Museum of Art across Beretania. Come toward evening and the fig-eating mynahs that roost here nightly make the banyans' size obvious from the noise alone.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by the arrangement, four banyans ringing the park's central fountain. They stand in Thomas Square, across Beretania Street from the Honolulu Museum of Art.

trees.name: The Geometry Tree of Ala Moana Beach Park

location.address: Ala Moana Beach Park, 1201 Ala Moana Blvd, Honolulu, HI 96814

trees.access: Free, public city beach park, open 4am to 10pm daily, no admission.
trees.transport: Ala Moana Beach Park, between Waikiki and downtown Honolulu; TheBus stops along Ala Moana Blvd, and it borders Ala Moana Center, the shopping mall.
trees.verify_notes: Species, girth (320cm, checked consistent with the recorded 101.6cm diameter) and height (47ft/14.3m) come from the City and County of Honolulu's Exceptional Trees register (Act 105 of 1975, CC0), cross-checked against the department's own earlier printed survey of the same designation. Both are the same city program rather than fully independent sources, and no age is recorded anywhere, so this stays flagged. The register's coordinates are only grid-rounded to about 1.1km, so the pin marks the park itself (Wikipedia's own coordinate for the park matches the register's rounded point) rather than the tree's exact spot within it.
trees.story:
Ala Moana Beach Park has roughly forty banyans planted for its 1937 Banyan Garden, and one tree in the park belongs to none of them. Officially it is a Black Olive, Bucida buceras, but it earned its nickname, the Geometry Tree, from the way it grows: branches stack outward in flat, level tiers rather than the tangled shape most trees settle into. Some Black Olives are pruned hard to force that look; this one has done most of the work on its own.

The species is native to the Caribbean and Central America and arrived in Hawaii as a landscaping ornamental, prized for exactly this tiered habit. The City and County of Honolulu designated it an Exceptional Tree under the state's 1975 tree-protection law, recording a trunk just over three metres round and a crown reaching about fourteen metres, rated in excellent health at its last survey.

Ala Moana itself has been public land since the 1930s, built from reclaimed wetland into Honolulu's busiest beach park, free to enter every day between four in the morning and ten at night. No ticket, no gate, and the tree stands among the park's open lawns rather than off any marked path, worth hunting down once you know the odd, stacked shape to look for.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the branches, stacked outward in flat level tiers rather than tangled. It stands on the open lawns of Ala Moana Beach Park, apart from the forty banyans of the Banyan Garden.

trees.name: The UH Manoa Art Building Baobab

location.address: University of Hawaii at Manoa, Art Building, 2535 McCarthy Mall, Honolulu, HI 96822

trees.access: Free, public university campus. UH Manoa's outdoor grounds and campus walkways (including McCarthy Mall) are open to the public without admission; the tree stands beside the Art Building's exterior, not inside it.
trees.transport: On the UH Manoa campus; nearest TheBus stops on University Ave/Dole St, short walk (about 10 minutes) onto campus to McCarthy Mall.
trees.verify_notes: Register: Hawaii Exceptional Trees list, id 1294, species Adansonia digitata, locality 'UHM campus near Art building', vitality Excellent, no girth/height recorded in that row. UH's own 2023 arboretum news piece says UH Manoa is home to 'the largest Baobab tree in the United States', located at the Art Building, 2535 McCarthy Mall, and that the building was designed around the then-30-year-old tree when Gilmore Hall (built 1935) was demolished in 1973, implying the tree predates 1943 and was already established by 1935. ilind.net (2019, local Honolulu civic blogger) independently corroborates: a photo from around 1972 shows the tree already mature beside old Gilmore Hall before demolition; UH art faculty and students insisted the tree be saved and the new building built around it. edohawaii.com gives a tree-specific coordinate (21.2994, -157.81798) and photos of people at the base for scale. Age: 'the then 30-year-old tree' in 1973 is UH's own figure via secondary sources, not a planting record; treated loosely as circa-1943 planting giving roughly 80-90 years by 2026, kept broad rather than sharpened. No measured girth found in any source. Distinct from the Ala Moana Beach Park baobab grove (an ensemble with no single standout specimen, set aside as not a collectible point) and from Foster Botanical Garden's baobab (already published as hnl_001). Alive-now evidence: UH's own arboretum feature, published 2023-04-21, describes the tree in the present tense as a current campus landmark.
trees.story:
When the University of Hawaii tore down Gilmore Hall in 1973, one thing did not move. Art faculty and students had grown fond of the baobab already standing beside the old building, and when its replacement went up, the tree stayed exactly where it was and the new Art Building was built around it. More than fifty years later it still stands pressed against the exterior wall, close enough that photographs make it look almost part of the structure.

The University calls it the largest baobab in the United States, and the claim is plausible: baobabs are native to Africa and Madagascar and rarely reach this size far outside the tropics they evolved in, let alone on a university campus in the middle of the Pacific. The tree was already about 30 years old when the building rose around it, which puts its planting somewhere in the early 1940s, before Hawaii became a state.

Nobody has taped its girth for the record, and no register lists one. What survives instead is the story everyone on campus already knows: a tree stubborn enough, and loved enough, that an entire building changed shape to keep it standing.

trees.name: The Sinclair Cannonball Tree

location.address: University of Hawaii at Manoa campus, near Bachman Hall / the visitor parking area, makai of Sinclair Library, Honolulu, HI 96822

trees.access: Free, public university campus. UH Manoa's outdoor grounds are open to the public without admission; the tree stands in open campus landscaping near Bachman Hall / Sinclair Library, not inside any building.
trees.transport: On the UH Manoa campus; nearest TheBus stops on University Ave/Dole St, short walk (about 10 minutes) onto campus.
trees.verify_notes: Register: Hawaii Exceptional Trees list, id 119, locality 'University of Hawaii - Manoa, Sinclair Library', girth 313.9cm, height ~18m, vitality Good. hawaii.edu itself unreachable from this environment; used the Wayback Machine's archived copies of UH Botany faculty member G. Carr's 'Campus Plants' pages instead (independently fetchable, UH's own primary source): page8.htm places it 'Makai of visitor's parking kiosk, Ewa-mauka of Bachman'; page14.htm cross-references it as a landmark between Bachman Hall and Sinclair Library, consistent with the register locality. Alive-now: UH News's own 'Image of the Week: Cannonball flower' (archived, dated 2025-01-15) is recent, dated, first-party evidence of blooming. A widely repeated claim that it was planted in 1933 by playwright Thornton Wilder appears only in search-summary form on unreachable hawaii.edu pages and is not used per the search-summary-is-a-lead rule; age left empty. No tree-level coordinate exists; pin anchored on Bachman Hall's geocoded building coordinate as the nearest fixed point and marked approximate.
trees.story:
Its flowers grow straight out of the trunk, and so, eventually, does fruit the size of cannonballs. Couroupita guianensis is native to the rainforests of Guiana, and on the UH Manoa campus, tucked between Bachman Hall and Sinclair Library near the visitor parking kiosk, one specimen has grown a trunk 314 centimetres round with the species' strange, tangled flower stems still running down its bark.

The flowers themselves are large, fragrant and short-lived, which is presumably why UH's own news office photographed one in bloom for its January 2025 'Image of the Week'. The fruit that follows is genuinely cannonball-sized, round and hard-shelled, and it drops rather than clings, so anyone standing directly underneath should keep half an eye up.

No age is recorded for this tree anywhere UH has published. A widely repeated claim online says it was planted in 1933 by the playwright Thornton Wilder during a stint teaching at the university; it could not be independently confirmed this pass, so it is left out rather than repeated on faith. Free to see, on open campus ground, a short walk from Sinclair Library.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the tangled flower stems running down the bark of a trunk 314 centimetres round. It stands between Bachman Hall and Sinclair Library, near the visitor parking kiosk.

trees.name: The Nuuanu Valley Monkeypod

location.address: Nuuanu Valley Park, 2925 Pali Highway, Honolulu, HI 96817

trees.access: Free, public city park. Nuuanu Valley Park is a public playground and picnic park on Pali Highway, open to all, with its own parking lot.
trees.transport: About 3-4 km from downtown Honolulu up Pali Highway; TheBus route 4 runs along Pali Highway, or roughly 10-15 minutes by car from downtown.
trees.verify_notes: Register: Hawaii Exceptional Trees list, id 1208, locality 'Nuuanu Park', girth 585.2cm, height ~15.5m, vitality Excellent. A second, adjacent register entry (id 1207, Chinese Banyan, same locality, 1332cm girth) is a lead, not shipped: no independent write-up naming that specific banyan was found. honolulumagazine.com's Playground Guide to Nuuanu Valley Park independently confirms the address as a free public park with 'enormous monkeypod trees', describing gigantic lower branches low enough that children climb them, with a rock placed underneath one to help access it. A separate honolulumagazine.com exceptional-trees gallery independently corroborates the park as a real, current Exceptional Tree site (naming a different registered mango there). Alive-now: a 2026-09-01 Hawaii Public Radio storm-damage roundup on Oahu's exceptional trees named other sites with storm losses and did not mention Nuuanu Park, the best available signal though not proof. Species named 'Monkeypod' locally, matched to Rain Tree (Samanea saman) per hard rule 9's canonical-name convention already used for Kauai and Singapore. No age or planting record found; girth alone cannot fix one honestly for a fast-growing species, so left empty.
trees.story:
Someone has wedged a rock under one of the low branches here, presumably to help visitors reach it, because the rain trees of Nuuanu Valley Park, known locally as monkeypods, grow their canopy close enough to the ground that children climb, sit and walk along the branches themselves. The largest carries a trunk 585 centimetres round, registered by the City and County of Honolulu as an Exceptional Tree and rated in excellent health.

The rain tree, Samanea saman, is native to Central and South America and was brought to Hawaii as shade. It grows fast and wide rather than tall, which is exactly what makes its low, spreading branches so easy to reach. Nuuanu Valley Park itself sits a short drive up Pali Highway from downtown Honolulu, an ordinary public playground and picnic ground with its own parking lot, and a second Exceptional Tree, an enormous banyan more than thirteen metres round, grows in the same park.

No age or planting record survives, and girth alone cannot fix one honestly for a fast-growing species like this. Free, open, no ticket, and the shade is the point.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the low spreading branches, close enough to the ground to sit on, with a rock wedged under one of them. It stands in Nuuanu Valley Park on a trunk 585 centimetres round.

trees.name: The Iolani Palace Banyan

location.address: Iolani Palace grounds, 364 S. King St., Honolulu, HI 96813 (mauka/inland side of the grounds)

trees.access: Free. The 11-acre Iolani Palace grounds are open to the public without a ticket (Tue-Sat; check iolanipalace.org for current hours); only the guided tour of the palace interior requires paid admission.
trees.transport: TheBus routes serve downtown Honolulu; Iolani Palace is about a 10-minute walk from the Aloha Tower / Chinatown area.
trees.story:
The register gives this banyan a girth of nearly twenty-two metres. That number is not one trunk. Roughly sixteen major trunks have fused around the original stem and the tape goes round the whole cluster, which is how an Indian banyan works: aerial roots come down, thicken, root, and become trunks in their own right until one tree occupies a courtyard.

It is the most prominent tree on the mauka side of the Iolani Palace grounds. Who put it there is disputed. One account credits Queen Kapiolani with planting it; another says it arrived as a gift from Indian royalty to King Kalakaua, with Kapiolani again doing the planting. Both point at the same window, the early 1880s, when Kalakaua was building the palace itself between 1879 and 1882. That gives roughly 140 years, and the band stays wide because the planter is genuinely in question even though the era is not.

So the tree is about as old as the palace it shades, and it was already large when the Hawaiian Kingdom was overthrown in 1893. Cuttings from it were reportedly carried to Kailua Bay in Kona and to Hulihe'e Palace.

It is still in service. The palace rents the ground beneath it as the Banyan Terrace, so people now get married under a tree a queen is said to have planted.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the cluster of roughly sixteen fused trunks, close to twenty-two metres round the whole ring. It stands on the mauka side of the Iolani Palace grounds, the most prominent tree there.

trees.name: The Queen's Medical Center Pink Bombax

location.address: The Queen's Medical Center grounds, near the roundabout, 1301 Punchbowl St., Honolulu, HI 96813

trees.access: Free. Queen's Medical Center's outdoor grounds (a hospital campus) are open to the public; the tree stands outdoors near the roundabout, not inside any building.
trees.transport: TheBus routes serve Punchbowl St; about a 10-minute walk from Iolani Palace / downtown Honolulu.
trees.story:
For a few days in late March this tree covers itself in pink flowers shaped like shaving brushes, garish enough that Honolulu Magazine reached for exactly that word. The new leaves follow deep red and only settle into green later, and while the tree is actively growing the bark takes on a green tone and visibly swells.

It was planted by William Hillebrand, the German botanist who served as royal physician in nineteenth-century Honolulu and whose kapok still stands in Foster Botanical Garden. The reason is on record: Queen Emma wanted the hospital grounds to be welcoming to the people who came to them, and Hillebrand planted to that brief. Honolulu Magazine puts the tree at more than 150 years old, which is the only figure anybody offers. Read it as a floor rather than a measurement, because nobody has narrowed it since.

The trunk has been taped once, by the city's Exceptional Trees register, at 3.75 metres round, with its condition rated good. That single entry is the whole measurement record.

It stands to the right of the roundabout on the Queen's Medical Center campus, a working hospital whose outdoor grounds anybody can walk through, a few minutes from Iolani Palace. Fifty weeks of the year it is a well-shaped green tree on a hospital lawn. The last week of March is the one to put in the diary.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the bark, green-toned and visibly swollen when the tree is growing, and in late March by pink flowers like shaving brushes. It stands right of the roundabout on the Queen's Medical Center grounds.

best_time.label: late March, when it flowers in garish pink shaving brushes

trees.name: The Queen's Medical Center Baobab

location.address: The Queen's Medical Center grounds, 1301 Punchbowl St., Honolulu, HI 96813

trees.access: Free. Queen's Medical Center's outdoor grounds (a hospital campus) are open to the public; the tree stands outdoors on the street-facing grounds.
trees.transport: TheBus routes serve Punchbowl St; about a 10-minute walk from Iolani Palace / downtown Honolulu.
trees.story:
A sign in Foster Botanical Garden sends visitors away from its own baobab. The oldest baobab in town, it says, is not the one in the garden but this one, under a mile away on the lawn of a working hospital.

Older, then, but not bigger. This trunk goes 11.8 metres round and Foster's is thicker still, so the claim rests entirely on age, and age is the one thing nobody has. The city's Exceptional Trees register records the species, the girth and a condition of good, and leaves the age blank. The enthusiast survey that has catalogued Honolulu's baobabs one by one, and that walked here with a hand-held GPS to fix the spot on the ground, found no planting date either. A second Honolulu photographer gets as far as massive and ancient. So nobody has dated this tree. If you know when it went in, tell us and it goes on the page.

What is not in question is the bulk. Adansonia digitata puts on that kind of trunk largely to hold water through a dry African season it will never meet on Punchbowl Street, and having been planted somewhere it never has to ration anything, it has simply kept going. It stands outdoors on the street side of the hospital grounds, free to walk up to, ten minutes from Iolani Palace.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 11.8 metres round. It stands outdoors on the street-facing grounds of the Queen's Medical Center; the campus's other listed tree, the pink bombax by the roundabout, is a third as thick.

trees.name: The Zoo Gate Banyans

location.address: Outside the main entrance to the Honolulu Zoo, 151 Kapahulu Ave., Honolulu, HI 96815 (in Queen Kapiolani Park, not inside the ticketed zoo)

trees.access: Free. These banyans stand outside the zoo's ticket gate, in the public grounds of Kapiolani Park; no zoo admission is needed to reach or sit under them.
trees.transport: TheBus routes serve Kapahulu Ave / Kalakaua Ave; about a 15-20 minute walk from central Waikiki.
trees.story:
The best tree at the Honolulu Zoo is outside the ticket gate. Two banyans flank the entrance on Kapahulu Avenue, standing in the public grounds of Kapiolani Park rather than in the zoo, and benches have been built in a ring around the trunk of the seaward one. Sitting under it costs nothing.

The city's Exceptional Trees register carries them as two separate entries, the mauka tree and the makai tree. That is bookkeeping rather than something a visitor experiences: walk up to the gate and it is one cluster of banyans over one entrance, which is how the Historic Hawaii Foundation describes it too. The makai tree's measurements are the ones worth quoting, 16.5 metres round and a little over five metres across the trunk. Its neighbour's numbers contradict each other in the register and are best left alone until somebody re-measures.

Neither has been dated. Banyans arrived in Hawaii in the late 1800s as a species, but that is a fact about the species and not a planting date for these two, and no register or historic listing supplies one. If you know, tell us.

An Indian banyan does not grow upward so much as outward. Aerial roots drop, thicken and set as trunks, and the tree walks across the ground over decades. These two have had long enough to throw shade over the whole entrance, and over everyone queuing to pay.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by the ring of benches built around the trunk of the seaward tree, 16.5 metres round. They stand outside the Honolulu Zoo's ticket gate on Kapahulu Avenue, one either side of the entrance.

trees.name: The Moana Banyan

location.address: 2365 Kalakaua Avenue, Waikiki, Honolulu, HI 96815 (the Banyan Court, the hotel's oceanfront courtyard, Moana Surfrider hotel)

trees.access: Free to view. The Banyan Court is the hotel's open oceanfront courtyard; non-guests may walk through it and the adjoining Beach Bar is open to the general public, but it sits inside a working hotel (Moana Surfrider, a Westin Resort) rather than a park.
trees.transport: Central Waikiki, on Kalakaua Ave; TheBus routes along Kalakaua Ave stop within a couple of minutes' walk; walkable from any Waikiki hotel.
trees.story:
This banyan was already seven years old when somebody planted it, and it was about seven feet tall. That was 1904, and the man with the spade was Jared Smith, who ran the territory's Department of Agriculture experiment station. He put it into the seafront courtyard of the Moana hotel on Waikiki beach.

It now stands around 23 metres high and throws its crown about 46 metres across, which is another way of saying the tree ate the courtyard. The courtyard is named after it. Everything that has happened in the Banyan Court for a century, and Waikiki has done a great deal of happening in that time, has happened under this tree. In 1979 it was among the first names on Hawaii's Rare and Exceptional Tree List, and it was later designated a Millennium Landmark Tree.

One number here is worth distrusting. The city register gives this tree a girth of 45.7 metres, which is exactly 150 feet, which is exactly the canopy spread every other source reports. That is a mislabelled column rather than a trunk, so we have left the girth blank instead of repeating a spread as a waistline. If you have put a tape around it, tell us.

The Banyan Court is open to walk through whether you are staying at the hotel or not, and the bar under the branches serves anyone.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the fact that it is the courtyard: one banyan about 23 metres high with a crown 46 metres wide, filling the Moana Surfrider's oceanfront Banyan Court between the hotel and the beach.

trees.name: The International Market Place Banyan
trees.age_estimate: at least a century old; one account says planted around 1850

location.address: 2330 Kalakaua Avenue, Waikiki, Honolulu, HI 96815 (centre of the International Market Place, under the open-air lattice canopy structure)

trees.access: Free. Stands at the centre of the open-air International Market Place shopping centre in Waikiki, publicly walkable with no ticket or entry fee.
trees.transport: Central Waikiki, on Kalakaua Ave; TheBus routes along Kalakaua/Kuhio stop within a few minutes' walk.
trees.story:
Don the Beachcomber ran his office out of this tree. In the 1950s the restaurateur Donn Beach had a workspace built up in the branches of the banyan at the centre of the International Market Place, and the tree has outlasted him and two versions of the shopping centre around it.

How old it is depends on who you ask, and the gap is wide enough to notice. Hawaii Magazine and Wikipedia both settle for a century old. Honolulu Magazine tells a longer story: planted in the mid-1850s by the New Zealand entrepreneur Harry Macfarlane, on ground that later belonged to King Lunalilo, who died there in 1874, and after him to Queen Emma. That version makes it about 170. We have not picked a winner, so the honest answer is somewhere between 100 and 176 years, and it was standing here long before the market place opened around it in 1957.

What is not in dispute is 2013. The whole place was demolished and rebuilt at a cost in the hundreds of millions, and the banyan stayed. The new open-air canopy was engineered to route its steel around the tree rather than take the tree out, and an arborist looks it over daily. That arborist, Steve Nimz, has been minding it since 1971.

It is free to walk up to, in the open middle of the shops on Kalakaua Avenue.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the roof: the lattice canopy over the International Market Place was built to bend around this one tree. It stands alone at the centre of the open-air mall, off Kalakaua Avenue.

trees.name: The Skunk Tree of UH Manoa

location.address: University of Hawaii at Manoa campus, near George Hall, 2560 Campus Road, Honolulu, HI 96822

trees.access: Free, public university campus. UH Manoa's outdoor grounds and campus walkways are open to the public without admission; the tree stands in open campus landscaping near George Hall, not inside any building. Same access basis as hnl_009 and hnl_010, already published for this campus.
trees.transport: On the UH Manoa campus; nearest TheBus stops on University Ave/Dole St, short walk (about 10 minutes) onto campus.
trees.story:
Once a year part of the University of Hawaii's Manoa campus starts to smell like a stable, and it takes people a while to work out why. The source is this one. Sterculia foetida flowers once a year, the flowers stink for about three weeks, and the Latin means foul-smelling; the campus calls it the skunk tree. A library staffer told the student paper that on a hot, humid day the smell settles into the open space and sits there. Richard Criley, emeritus professor of tropical plant and soil sciences, was kinder: this is one of the sort of tree that calls attention to itself.

When to catch it is not settled. The Ka Leo O Hawaii feature that put all this on the record in 2019 has it blooming around that May, while other accounts give a January to March window, so pick your month at your own risk. Nobody has dated the tree either. The city register gives a trunk 2.9 metres round on a tree only about 7.5 metres tall, condition good, and no age at all.

Nor is it perfectly clear which tree. The register puts its entry near George Hall. The same student feature describes two skunk trees on campus, one by Sinclair Library and one beside the Architecture Building, and names neither as George Hall. All of those stand a few hundred metres apart, so the pin sits on George Hall and says approximate. In flower, your nose will settle it.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it in flower by the smell, and otherwise by a trunk 2.9 metres round on a tree only about 7.5 metres tall. It stands in open landscaping near George Hall; a second skunk tree grows elsewhere on campus.

trees.name: The Kuhio Beach Hula Mound Banyan

location.address: Kuhio Beach Park, beside the Hula Mound and the Duke Kahanamoku Statue, Kalakaua Avenue, Waikiki, Honolulu, HI 96815

verified_sources: https://data.honolulu.gov/Community/Exceptional-Trees/84fd-3fzf (City & County of Honolulu, Exceptional Trees register, Act 105 of 1975, CC0; register id 391, Ficus benghalensis, Kuhio Beach Park, girth 4053.8 cm, height 70 ft, vitality Good)

https://www.openstreetmap.org/node/5216796590 (OSM node individually tagged genus=Ficus, denotation=natural_monument, last checked by a mapper 2026-03-29, at 21.2749708,-157.8248207, ~60m from the Duke Kahanamoku Statue beside the Hula Mound)
https://thishawaiilife.com/kuhio-beach-park/ (describes the 'giant banyan tree' at Kuhio Beach as the site of free Saturday-evening hula and music performances)
trees.access: Free, always open. Kuhio Beach Park is a public city beach park in central Waikiki with no gate and no entry fee.
trees.transport: In central Waikiki, an easy walk (under 15 minutes) from the Moana Banyan and the International Market Place Banyan already on this page; TheBus routes 8, 19, 20 and 23 and the Waikiki Trolley stop on Kalakaua Ave nearby.
trees.story:
The register puts forty metres of circumference around this tree, and not one centimetre of it is a trunk.

Banyans grow sideways and downward. The limbs throw out aerial roots, the roots reach the sand and thicken into pillars, and the pillars fuse into a mass that a tape measure has to treat as one object because there is no honest way to treat it as several. Honolulu's exceptional tree register, set up under a 1975 state law that let the counties protect individual trees by name, records this one at 4,053.8 centimetres around and about 21 metres tall, vitality good. That circumference is the whole fused base rather than a stem, and it cannot be turned into an age: growth rate dating assumes a single trunk, and nothing about a banyan is single.

So nobody knows how old it is. No planting date has surfaced anywhere, which is a strange gap for a tree with a stage underneath it.

The Hula Mound sits directly beneath the crown, on Kuhio Beach, and on Saturday evenings the free hula and music shows run there with the banyan as the roof. The Duke Kahanamoku statue stands about sixty metres up the sand. No gate, no ticket, no closing time.

If anyone has a date for it, we will take it.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the aerial roots dropping from the limbs and thickening into extra trunks, forty metres round the fused base. It stands over the Kuhio Beach Hula Mound, sixty metres from the Duke Kahanamoku statue.
